title: Range Queries Need an Index Too
description: A BETWEEN range on an unindexed column scans; a B-tree index serves ranges as well as equality, seeking straight to the band. Why it matters: range filters (dates, prices, IDs) are everywhere in real screens, and this exact gap is why a report that's fast today grinds to a halt as the table grows.
narrative:
## Scenario
An HR screen lists employees in a narrow salary band. There's no index on `Salary`, so finding ~170 people forces SQL Server to read all 200,000 rows.

## Why it's slow
A `BETWEEN` is a **range predicate**. Without a suitable index, the only way to satisfy it is a **Clustered Index Scan** — read every row and test each against the range. It works, but the cost grows with the whole table, not with how many rows match.

## What to look for
- A **Clustered Index Scan** of `Employees` with reads proportional to the full table.
- A tiny result set returned only after a full scan.

## The concept
An index isn't just for equality (`=`) lookups — because a B-tree keeps keys **in sorted order**, it's ideal for ranges (`BETWEEN`, `>`, `<`). Add a nonclustered index on `Salary` (INCLUDE the columns you return so it's covering) and the engine **seeks** to the start of the band and walks just the matching rows.
hints: There is no index on Salary, so the range test must scan every row.
A B-tree index stores keys in order, which makes it perfect for BETWEEN / > / < ranges, not just equality.
CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX IX_Employees_Salary ON Employees(Salary) INCLUDE (Name); then re-run the query.
